Snippet: Causal discovery refers to a set of methods aimed at learning the causal structure (i.e., the relationships between variables), directly from data, typically represented as a DAG. Unlike traditional approaches that assume a predefined causal structure (as is often the case in panel regressions or DAGs manually specified by experts), causal discovery infers the structure from observational data using algorithms. These include the PC algorithm (Spirtes and Glymour 1991) and its successors, as well as nonlinear methods like convergent cross mapping (CCM) (Runge 2023). For example, in a dataset including LULCC we might not even know whether LULCC is the origin of a causal relationship or the result, or at which scale a given variable is causal. At its simplest, causal discovery aims to identify sets of causal models that are statistically indistinguishable from each other (formally, they have the same Markov equivalence class) as they share common patterns of conditional independence with other variables (formally the same d-separation patterns) (Huber 2024). When observational data is insufficient to identify the correct causal model, the challenge of model ambiguity may be resolved by incorporating external sources of information. This can involve domain knowledge, theoretical principles, previous empirical findings, or knowledge of the temporal order of events (Huber 2024). These external insights can provide valuable context to constrain potential causal models. In practice, fully understanding all potential causal relationships for a complex DAG (e.g. for LULCC system) is challenging due to the complexities of the dependency structures of the variables (Huber 2024). Moreover, the assumptions on the functional relationships between variables and on the error terms are quite restrictive. This means causal discovery is inherently difficult, and if domain knowledge can be used to identify potential causal pathways in a DAG, this should be used rather than causal discovery. Title: IGDA: Interactive Graph Discovery through Large Language Model Agents
Snippet: Causal Discovery and LLMs. The causal discovery task involves learning causal relationships from observed empirical data (Peters et al., 2017;Spirtes & Zhang, 2016). Many proposed algorithms exist (Spirtes et al., 1993;Yu et al., 2019;Nauta et al., 2019;Zheng et al., 2018;Chickering, 2002) attempting to solve the causal discovery problem. However, these methods are known to struggle on real world graphs where observations are noisy or common structural assumptions are violated (Chevalley et al., 2023;Tu et al., 2019). 

Recently, LLMs have emerged as an alternative approach to causal discovery (Kıcıman et al., 2024;Abdulaal et al., 2024;Vashishtha et al., 2023;Li et al., 2024;Lampinen et al., 2023). Kıcıman et al. (2024) first investigated the capability of LLMs to act as zero-shot causal discovery agents using only semantic information and pairwise prompting on each variable pair. Follow-up work (Abdulaal et al., 2024) further improves LLM predictions with observational data by selecting for predictions which maximize data likelihood. Vashishtha et al. (2023) utilize triplet prompting to prevent cycles when the causal graph is acyclic. They show only a topological ordering on variables is required for many common causal reasoning tasks (Chu et al., 2023). 

Other works (Zhou et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2024) benchmark LLMs across a range of causality related tasks including causal discovery and causal inference confirming that LLMs struggle with integrating numerical data. 

Another line of work more related to our proposed interactive causal discovery problem studies how to incorporate background knowledge into causal discovery algorithms (Meek, 2013). Define a set of background knowledge as the tuple K = (F, R), where F specifies a set of "forbidden" graph edges and R specifies a set of "required" graph edges. # What “distribution shift under interventions” means

Interventions change the data-generating process in ways distinct from passive observation, producing interventional distributions P(V; σ) that differ from the observational P(V). Hard (“do-”) interventions set variables to values or distributions independent of their parents, while soft (“shift/scale/mechanism”) interventions preserve causal edges but alter the conditional distributions or structural equations of target variables; both yield different joint distributions and counterfactual targets under the same causal model M = (G, Θ) <cite id="0e1f6cdb-0">Interventions are an effective way to represent distribution shifts in a causal model; applying an intervention σ changes the joint distribution P(V) to an interventional distribution P(V; σ), distinct from the observational P(V)</cite> <cite id="0e1f6cdb-2">Shift interventions add a fixed amount or scale values while preserving causal edges into X; perfect do-interventions are a special case; the resulting interventional distribution is the shift-scale counterfactual distribution</cite>. Treatment effect statements formalize counterfactual outcomes under hypothetical interventions; “dose response with distribution shift” explicitly considers alternative populations with shifted data distributions, linking causal effects to interventional targets across shifted settings <cite id="0e1f6cdb-1">Treatment effects are counterfactual outcomes under hypothetical interventions; “dose response with distribution shift” defines the counterfactual mean outcome under D = d for an alternative population with shifted distribution P</cite>.

# How causal discovery addresses distribution shift under interventions

Causal discovery leverages structure and invariances to separate stable mechanisms from shifted factors, enabling identification and prediction under interventions. Two intervention notions are central: hard interventions that sever links to parents (mechanism replacement) and soft interventions that preserve edges but change functional forms; interventional data with mechanism changes are “very valuable” for inferring causal relations and exploiting changes to reveal structure under distribution shift <cite id="8e077e6c-1">Hard interventions disrupt dependence on parents (fix values stochastically or deterministically), while soft interventions preserve dependence but alter mechanisms; interventional data with mechanism changes are valuable for causal discovery</cite> <cite id="8e077e6c-2">Changes like equipment/setting shifts often correspond to imperfect (mechanism) interventions; controlled experiments are perfect; invariance-based causal discovery is appealing because it can work with unknown interventions and identify parents even if indirectly affected</cite>.

A core strategy is to find representations or subsets of predictors whose relationships are invariant across environments (interventions/shifts). Anchor regression and related invariance-based methods explicitly exploit invariant dependencies across interventions or perturbations for causal inference and prediction; under shifted distributions due to interventions on variables entering the target equation linearly, invariance yields attractive guarantees, though exact invariance can be conservative and hurt performance on observational or moderately shifted data, motivating distributionally robust trade-offs <cite id="8e077e6c-0">Invariance across interventions/perturbations has been exploited for causal inference; interventions that shift the distribution of a target variable (affecting linear targets) admit invariance-based guarantees, but exact invariance can be conservative and reduce performance; robust prediction/estimation formulations trade off observational and shifted performance with optimality guarantees over specified perturbation classes</cite>. Causal domain adaptation strategies further tailor prediction to shifted mechanisms. Graph surgery/pruning enforce cross-domain invariance by removing unstable mechanisms or selecting predictor subsets that yield invariant conditionals, aligning with interventional targets (e.g., transportability), while acknowledging trade-offs: enforcing invariance can reduce information bias but may require counterfactual estimation or face scalability limits <cite id="4562da88-2">Causal methods guard against distributional shifts: transportability uses do-calculus to carry over interventional/observational effects; invariant causal prediction finds predictors with invariant residuals; graph surgery enforces cross-domain invariance; graph pruning selects invariant conditionals—though invariant predictors reduce transfer bias, scalability and estimation burdens remain</cite> <cite id="4562da88-3">Under covariate shift across source and target domains, potential outcomes may satisfy p(Y(t)|X)=pπ(Y(t)|X); selection on invariant conditionals ties treatment models to domain-invariant mechanisms for adapting effect estimation</cite>. The two fields meet via shared primitives: invariances across environments, interventional targets, and worst-case distributional risk. Invariance-based causal discovery (e.g., ICP variants, anchor regression) supplies features/representations that are stable under interventions or perturbations, which can then be used as inputs to conformal procedures to obtain coverage-valid prediction sets under covariate/label shift and even under known interventions; worst-case losses from robust CP align with causal robustness and can be cast as distributionally robust objectives over interventional distributions <cite id="8e077e6c-0">Invariance across interventions/perturbations underlies causal prediction, with distributionally robust formulations trading off performance across shift classes and yielding robust losses for identifying functionals</cite> <cite id="4562da88-0">Weighted conformal prediction under covariate/label shift uses importance weights to achieve marginal/conditional coverage, and meta/adaptive CP extend guarantees to nonstationary mixtures</cite>. - When interventions are controllable or partially known, design CP around interventional targets P(V; σ): use known σ to update distributions for reweighting or to construct interventional prediction sets; combine with causal discovery to detect/learn mechanisms that remain invariant across intervention classes for robust coverage <cite id="0e1f6cdb-0">Interventions σ define P(V; σ), enabling interventional distribution-based reweighting or prediction</cite> <cite id="4562da88-0">Weighted CP uses importance weights to achieve desired coverage under covariate/label shift, supplying a template for intervention-aware reweighting</cite>.

Hard (“do-”) interventions set variables to values or distributions independent of their parents, while soft (“shift/scale/mechanism”) interventions preserve causal edges but alter the conditional distributions or structural equations of target variables; both yield different joint distributions and counterfactual targets under the same causal model M = (G, Θ) <cite id="0e1f6cdb-0">Interventions are an effective way to represent distribution shifts in a causal model; applying an intervention σ changes the joint distribution P(V) to an interventional distribution P(V; σ), distinct from the observational P(V)</cite> <cite id="0e1f6cdb-2">Shift interventions add a fixed amount or scale values while preserving causal edges into X; perfect do-interventions are a special case; the resulting interventional distribution is the shift-scale counterfactual distribution</cite>. Treatment effect statements formalize counterfactual outcomes under hypothetical interventions; “dose response with distribution shift” explicitly considers alternative populations with shifted data distributions, linking causal effects to interventional targets across shifted settings <cite id="0e1f6cdb-1">Treatment effects are counterfactual outcomes under hypothetical interventions; “dose response with distribution shift” defines the counterfactual mean outcome under D = d for an alternative population with shifted distribution P</cite>.

# How causal discovery addresses distribution shift under interventions

Causal discovery leverages structure and invariances to separate stable mechanisms from shifted factors, enabling identification and prediction under interventions. A core strategy is to find representations or subsets of predictors whose relationships are invariant across environments (interventions/shifts). Anchor regression and related invariance-based methods explicitly exploit invariant dependencies across interventions or perturbations for causal inference and prediction; under shifted distributions due to interventions on variables entering the target equation linearly, invariance yields attractive guarantees, though exact invariance can be conservative and hurt performance on observational or moderately shifted data, motivating distributionally robust trade-offs <cite id="8e077e6c-0">Invariance across interventions/perturbations has been exploited for causal inference; interventions that shift the distribution of a target variable (affecting linear targets) admit invariance-based guarantees, but exact invariance can be conservative and reduce performance; robust prediction/estimation formulations trade off observational and shifted performance with optimality guarantees over specified perturbation classes</cite>. When multiple environments are observed, identifiability of causal graphs can be improved by assuming a shared mixing mechanism f with shifted source distributions p_iθ across auxiliary environments; under such models, identifiable graphs are those uniquely specified by cross-environmental distributions, providing a formal bridge from multi-environment data to causal structure recovery under shift <cite id="8e077e6c-4">In multiple-environment ICA/SCM settings, the mixing function f is invariant across environments while source distributions p_iθ shift; identifiability requires that the causal graph is uniquely specified by the joint distribution across these environments</cite>. Efficient algorithms like fastICP leverage invariance and minimum error testing to identify direct causal parents even when interventions are unknown or only partially applied, scaling beyond classic ICP and aiding robust representation learning and adaptive prediction under shift <cite id="8e077e6c-2">Invariance-based methods need no precise knowledge of intervention locations/effects; they can identify all parents even if indirectly affected by interventions, and do so efficiently (MMSE-ICP and fastICP), aiding robust representation learning and adaptive models under distribution shift</cite>.

Causal domain adaptation strategies further tailor prediction to shifted mechanisms. # How conformal prediction addresses distribution shift under interventions

Classical conformal prediction (CP) assumes exchangeability (i.i.d.) and provides marginal and conditional coverage guarantees (PAC-style) for prediction sets; under distribution shift, these guarantees break, motivating targeted extensions. The two fields meet via shared primitives: invariances across environments, interventional targets, and worst-case distributional risk. - When interventions are controllable or partially known, design CP around interventional targets P(V; σ): use known σ to update distributions for reweighting or to construct interventional prediction sets; combine with causal discovery to detect/learn mechanisms that remain invariant across intervention classes for robust coverage <cite id="0e1f6cdb-0">Interventions σ define P(V; σ), enabling interventional distribution-based reweighting or prediction</cite> <cite id="4562da88-0">Weighted CP uses importance weights to achieve desired coverage under covariate/label shift, supplying a template for intervention-aware reweighting</cite>.
- When shifts are unknown or heterogeneous, prefer invariance-based causal discovery (ICP/anchors, multi-environment identifiability) to extract stable predictors, then apply CP on the invariant representation for coverage; quantify trade-offs between observational and shifted performance (robust CP/estimation) <cite id="8e077e6c-0">Invariance-based guarantees are attractive but conservative; robust prediction/estimation trade off performance across observational and shifted data with optimality guarantees</cite> <cite id="8e077e6c-4">Identifiability with multiple environments relies on invariant mixing mechanisms under shifted sources, enabling invariant predictors for robust conformalization</cite>.

# Limitations and open issues

Exact invariance assumptions in causal discovery can be too strong; pragmatic robust losses and reweighting in CP provide coverage under broader shift classes, but require accurate importance weights or mechanistic knowledge. Further work integrates interventional CP frameworks with scalable causal discovery, and develops sequential/adaptive conformalization that leverages causal structure to decide which parts of P(V; σ) to robustify.

In fact, changes (e.g. different equipments, locations, demographics, weathers) often arise naturally in distribution-shift data. Given their abundance, harnessing changes for CD would reveal insights useful for understanding and manipulating complex systems. However, exploiting changes in general is difficult as they are often imperfect interventions (merely altering the mechanism generating a variable) affecting some unknown variables. In contrast, controlled experiments are perfect interventions that fix designated variables to predetermined values (Tian & Pearl, 2001;Eberhardt & Scheines, 2007). As such, invariance-based CD methods are appealing because they can work with unknown interventions.
